name: Dong quai (Angelica sinensis root, by mouth)
short: Case report: INR more than doubled in a woman on warfarin after 4 weeks of dong quai; reviews list bleeding risk with blood thinners. One man grew breast tissue on dong quai pills.
text: Bleeding and blood thinners: a case report describes a 46-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation, stable on the anticoagulant warfarin, whose prothrombin time and INR more than doubled after she took dong quai for 4 weeks; no other cause was found, and her values returned to acceptable levels 1 month after she stopped the herb. The authors say phytochemical analyses found natural coumarin derivatives in dong quai, along with constituents with antithrombotic, phototoxic and carcinogenic effects (a statement about constituents, not harms observed in people), and that one animal study suggests an interaction with warfarin whose true mechanism remains unknown. Reviews of herb-drug interactions list bleeding when warfarin is combined with dong quai among plausible interactions and say case reports suggest an interaction between them, while cautioning that many such reports are sketchy; a structured review of Chinese herbal medicines with anticoagulant or antiplatelet drugs names dong quai among the herbs whose interactions mainly raise bleeding risk through added anticoagulant or antiplatelet effects, and a review of warfarin interactions lists Angelica sinensis among herbs with case reports of severe adverse effects such as bleeding. A review also lists dong quai among herbs with antiplatelet activity that may raise bleeding risk with aspirin and other anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs), noting that most such interaction information comes from individual case reports, animal studies and laboratory data, and a review of clopidogrel interactions states that danggui can enhance the adverse effects of clopidogrel on bleeding time (the abstract does not say whether this was seen in people). On the other side, a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study in healthy volunteers tested three herbs, including Angelica sinensis (25 volunteers per herb; results are given for 24 in the Angelica sinensis group), each taken for 3 weeks alone and for 3 weeks with aspirin: on the whole there was no clinically relevant effect on platelet and clotting function, adding the herbs to aspirin did not further increase aspirin's platelet inhibition, and there was no significant bleeding, although 2 of the 24 in the Angelica sinensis group showed reduced platelet clumping in response to one laboratory agent (arachidonic acid). In a Taiwanese case-crossover study of 1,209 people taking antiplatelet drugs who were admitted to hospital with new bleeding, concurrent use of a set of prespecified Chinese medicines that included dong quai showed no strong relationship with major bleeding (the abstract gives no estimate for dong quai alone). Separately, in a study of 64 people with ulcerative colitis divided into two groups, most platelet measures, which are raised in that disease, improved significantly in the group given an injected form of angelica sinensis (a different route) with routine treatment for 3 weeks, and changed little in the group given routine treatment alone; the authors conclude that the injection can significantly inhibit platelet activation, an antiplatelet effect. Hormone-like effects: a case report describes a man who developed breast enlargement (gynaecomastia) after taking dong quai pills, which the authors link to the phytoestrogen the herb contains. In a 24-week randomised placebo-controlled trial in 71 postmenopausal women, dong quai produced no oestrogen-like changes in the womb lining or vaginal cells; the abstract reports no adverse-event data. Breast cancer: in a laboratory study, a water extract of dong quai stimulated the growth of oestrogen-receptor-positive breast cancer cells, and the authors urged caution in women with breast cancer pending further study; in people, a Taiwanese insurance-claims case-control study of 34,262 people newly diagnosed with breast cancer found a weakly lower risk with Angelica sinensis use (adjusted odds ratio 0.95), and a cohort of 35,016 postmenopausal women in Washington State found that dong quai use was not associated with breast cancer risk. These are observational and laboratory data. Liver: a 2016 systematic review of liver injury from Chinese herbal medicines found Dang-Gui among the six most common ingredients of the multi-herb patent medicines and decoctions reported to cause liver injury. Most patients in the review (96.3%) recovered, one died and one was receiving a liver transplant; the abstract does not say which products those patients had taken and does not attribute any case to Dang-Gui itself.
